items.title: Roswell Rudd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998
items.q: by the time of Mozart, he’s the only guy that’s improvising.

ctx.x: Oh yes of course. When I first went to play in Europe, actually I went with a college band in ‘58, and played, and just drifted around and played over there, but I realized that improvised music was nothing new to Europeans. And if you had a gift for improvisation you would really, you would be paid special attention, because then you were sort of in the line of great European composers. Because well let’s go back to an earlier time in music, before there was not that much writing but music was rote music.…

place. Then later on, sort of in the high Baroque you get more and more emphasis on fixed ensembles and a whole lot of writing and stuff getting scripted out, and so eventually by the time of Mozart, he’s the only guy that’s improvising. The composer is the only guy doing his own fantasy and everybody else is — he’s scripting out his fantasy to everybody else, so there’s not a hell of a lot of improvisation going on with the individual players, there’s more emphasis on the composer’s improvisation. But at least…
Do you think it’s healthy for jazz that it has found its place in the college education system that we have Jazz at Lincoln Center and all of that?
